title: Area VIII review: High-Altitude Operations
intro: These questions mix the two Tasks of Area VIII, supplemental oxygen and pressurization. Most of them join both in one high flight, because a pressurization problem quickly becomes an oxygen problem.

questions.q: In a pressurized single at 24,000 ft, a controller fault means the system now holds only 2.9 psi differential. Sorting out a lower altitude with ATC keeps you at 24,000 ft for 50 minutes. Using the chart shown, what does 91.211 require?
options: The required crew uses oxygen for the last 20 minutes; the passengers need nothing
The required crew uses oxygen for the whole 50 minutes, since the cabin is at 14,000 ft
Each occupant must be provided with oxygen, since the airplane is above 15,000 ft
Nothing, because the cabin is still pressurized
questions.why: Cabin pressure is outside pressure plus the differential. The chart gives 5.7 psi at 24,000 ft, so 5.7 + 2.9 = 8.6 psi, which is the 14,000 ft row [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]]. 91.211 counts cabin pressure altitude. Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft, the crew uses oxygen for the part over 30 minutes: 50 - 30 = 20 minutes. Passengers come in only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. The 'whole 50 minutes' answer misses the words 'up to and including'; the whole-flight rule starts above 14,000 ft.

questions.q: Your pressurized airplane loses its pressurization at FL 240 over mountains. The MEA keeps you at 16,000 ft for the next 25 minutes. What does 91.211 now require?
options: You may wait 30 minutes before using oxygen, and the passengers need nothing
You must use oxygen the whole time, and each passenger must be provided with it
You and every passenger must wear oxygen the whole time
Nothing new, since the 91.211(b) descent supply covers this
questions.why: With the pressurization gone, the cabin pressure altitude is about 16,000 ft, and 91.211(a) follows the cabin. Above 14,000 ft the required crew must use oxygen the entire time; above 15,000 ft each occupant must be provided with it. The rule says provided, not that passengers must use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. The 30-minute allowance is only for cabin altitudes above 12,500 up to 14,000 ft. The 10-minute supply in 91.211(b) applies above FL 250 and is in addition to the oxygen paragraph (a) requires [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], so plan the bottle for staying high over terrain, not just for the way down.

questions.q: A pressurized airplane decompresses at FL 270. You pull on your diluter-demand mask. The regulator has Normal (automix) and 100 percent settings. Which setting do you use?
options: Normal, since the automix gives the right mix for the cabin altitude
100 percent
Normal at first, then 100 percent only if you feel symptoms
Off until the descent is set up, to save oxygen
questions.why: The PHAK recommends that crewmembers select 100 percent oxygen at high altitude on a demand or pressure-demand regulator [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]], and the AC drill after a decompression is mask on, check flow, breathe 100 percent oxygen [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Normal is tempting, but most regulators approved to 40,000 ft do not reach 100 percent oxygen until about 34,000 ft cabin altitude [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], so at 27,000 ft you would still be breathing a mix. Waiting for symptoms is a trap: impaired performance may be immediate [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

questions.q: You make a rapid descent after a partial pressurization failure. Partway down, the outside air pressure becomes higher than the cabin pressure. Which part of the system deals with that?
options: The vacuum relief in the safety valve, which lets outside air into the cabin
The pressure relief in the safety valve, which lets cabin air out
The outflow valve, which closes fully to hold cabin pressure
The sonic venturi, which limits the air coming in
questions.why: The cabin safety valve combines pressure relief, vacuum relief and dump. Vacuum relief keeps outside pressure from exceeding cabin pressure by letting outside air in [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. AC 61-107B calls it a negative pressure relief valve, used after a sudden decompression or in a rapid descent [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. Pressure relief is the opposite job: it keeps cabin pressure from going above the set differential over the outside pressure [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

questions.q: You will cruise a pressurized single at FL 250. Your backup oxygen is a portable kit, and it is stowed in the aft baggage compartment, which you can reach only from outside on the ground. What is wrong with this?
options: Portable oxygen must be readily accessible in flight, and after a rapid decompression at 25,000 ft you may have about 90 seconds
Nothing, since 91.211(b) asks for a descent supply only above FL 250
Nothing, as long as the bottle is fastened securely
Nothing, since you can descend below 12,500 ft before anyone needs oxygen
questions.why: If there is no fixed installation, portable oxygen equipment must be readily accessible during flight [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 gives 1.5 to 2.5 minutes of useful consciousness at 25,000 ft after a rapid decompression, and you assume the lower value: 1.5 x 60 = 90 seconds [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Fastening the bottle is required too [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]], but a secured bottle you cannot reach does not help. The 91.211(b) point is true at exactly FL 250 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], but legal does not make an unreachable bottle a plan.

questions.q: At FL 230 you notice the cabin altimeter reads 16,000 ft and is creeping up. No warning has sounded, your pulse oximeter still shows a normal reading, and you feel fine. What is the best action?
options: Wait until the oximeter reading starts to fall, then put on oxygen
Put on your oxygen now and start down; do not wait for the oximeter
Troubleshoot the controller first, since you feel fine and the oximeter is normal
Have the passengers put on oxygen; 91.211 asks only them to use it above 15,000 ft
questions.why: A slow decompression may not be noticed, and hypoxia dulls your ability to recognize it [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The FAA cautions against relying on a pulse oximeter alone, because waiting for the saturation to fall can let you become impaired first [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. With the cabin above 14,000 ft, the required crew must use oxygen the whole time, while passengers above 15,000 ft must only be provided with it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. If hypoxia is suspected, the AC recommends a descent below 10,000 ft MSL [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

questions.q: After a decompression at FL 250 and a descent, a passenger has a deep ache in her knee that gets worse when she moves it. She wants to stretch it and work it out. What do you tell her and do?
options: Stretching is fine; it is a cramp from sitting, so continue to the destination
Keep the knee still, stay on 100 percent oxygen, land as soon as possible and get her to an AME or hyperbaric specialist
Continue to the destination, since bends pain goes away below 10,000 ft
Land, and since the pain eased, have her see her family doctor next week
questions.why: Deep joint pain made worse by moving the joint is the bends, a form of decompression sickness [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. The PHAK says: mask on at 100 percent, descend and land as soon as possible, keep a painful joint still and do not try to work the pain out, and get help from an FAA medical officer, AME, military flight surgeon or hyperbaric medicine specialist, because a doctor not trained in aviation or hypobaric medicine may not know the problem [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Symptoms that ease in the descent are still a reason to land and be evaluated [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

questions.q: Intense smoke fills the cabin of your pressurized single at FL 230. Four people are aboard, but there are oxygen masks only for the two front seats. What does the AFH point you toward?
options: Dump the cabin pressure at altitude to clear the smoke; two masks are enough
Stay pressurized and level, since the pressurization air will clear any smoke
Turn the oxygen to full flow so everyone can share it, and hold altitude
Make an emergency descent, since depressurizing at altitude needs oxygen for everyone
questions.why: The pressurization air removes smoke, but if the smoke is intense you may need to depressurize at altitude only if oxygen is available for all occupants; otherwise make an emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. With no oxygen for the back seats, dumping the cabin at FL 230 would make them hypoxic. Extra oxygen flowing in a cabin with a fire is the wrong idea: with a fire at high altitude, AC 61-107B says to descend at once to an altitude that does not require oxygen [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-11d]].

questions.q: A friend with a new commercial certificate will fly an unpressurized turbocharged single to 17,500 ft using oxygen. Does 14 CFR 61.31(g) high-altitude training apply to him?
options: Yes, because he will fly above 12,500 ft
Yes, because any flight on supplemental oxygen needs the endorsement
No, it covers only pressurized airplanes with a ceiling above 25,000 ft, though the AC recommends the training for anyone above 10,000 ft
No, and the AC training is not meant for piston airplanes at all
questions.why: 61.31(g) applies to a pressurized aircraft whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. AC 61-107B notes that and highly recommends the same training for all pilots who fly above 10,000 ft MSL [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. The last choice is wrong: the AC says its training is meant mainly for reciprocating engine and turboprop airplanes [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

questions.q: At FL 240 a side window cracks with a bang and the cabin fills with a white mist. A passenger shouts 'Fire!' What is the mist most likely to be, and what comes first?
options: Smoke from an electrical fire; use the extinguisher first
Oxygen escaping from the masks; turn off the oxygen first
Fog from the sudden drop in temperature and change in humidity; masks on first
Air conditioning condensation; no action is needed
questions.why: In an explosive decompression the cabin fills with fog, dust or debris; the fog comes from the rapid drop in temperature and the change in relative humidity [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. The primary danger of a decompression is hypoxia, so quick use of the oxygen equipment comes first, then a rapid descent [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Reaching for the extinguisher first spends useful consciousness on the wrong problem.

questions.q: Your pressurized airplane decompresses rapidly at FL 250. The emergency descent averages about 3,000 fpm. If you dive first without oxygen, about how long until the cabin is below 12,500 ft, and what does that tell you?
options: About 4.2 minutes, inside the 3 to 5 minutes of useful consciousness, so dive first
About 4.2 minutes, much longer than the 1.5 minutes you plan on, so mask first
About 2.5 minutes, inside your useful consciousness, so dive first
About 8.3 minutes, so the 10-minute 91.211(b) supply is just enough
questions.why: With no pressurization the cabin follows the airplane down. (25,000 - 12,500) / 3,000 = 4.2 minutes. AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 gives 3 to 5 minutes at 25,000 ft, but only 1.5 to 2.5 minutes after a rapid decompression, and you assume the lower value [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. The '3 to 5 minutes' choice reads the wrong column. So the mask goes on first, in 5 seconds or less, and then you descend [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. 8.3 minutes is 25,000 / 3,000, the time to sea level.

questions.q: You plan FL 270 in a pressurized single. The backup oxygen for everyone, pilot included, is a continuous-flow system. What does AC 61-107B say about it?
options: Continuous flow is approved only to 18,000 ft, so you need masks
It is certificated to 41,000 ft but needs very careful attention above 25,000 ft, and pilots should use the masks meant for them
It is as safe as pressure demand, so no extra attention is needed
It must be replaced by a pressure-demand system above 25,000 ft
questions.why: AC 61-107B says continuous-flow systems are certificated up to 41,000 ft MSL, but their capabilities need very careful attention above 25,000 ft MSL. Pilot masks sometimes allow more flow than passenger masks, so pilots should use the masks meant for them [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. The 18,000 ft figure is the PHAK's masks-instead-of-cannulas line, not a limit on continuous flow [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. Pressure demand is the system the PHAK calls safe above 40,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

questions.q: You fly a Part 135 charter in a pressurized single at FL 230 with the cabin at 8,000 ft. Must the passenger briefing cover oxygen?
options: No, because the cabin altitude is only 8,000 ft
No, oxygen briefings are needed only in large or turbojet multiengine airplanes
Yes, because the flight involves operations above 12,000 ft MSL
Only if the flight spends more than 30 minutes above 12,000 ft
questions.why: Under 135.117 the briefing must cover the normal and emergency use of oxygen if the flight involves operations above 12,000 ft MSL [[6:36|14 CFR 135.117]]. FL 230 is above that, whatever the cabin altimeter says, and a decompression would bring the cabin up to the airplane. The large and turbojet multiengine airplane briefing is the Part 91 subpart F rule [[60:534|14 CFR 91.519]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]], not the Part 135 one.

questions.q: Why does the AFH preflight functional test of the oxygen system include talking to ATC through the mask microphone?
options: Because Part 91 requires a microphone in every oxygen mask
To measure the oxygen flow rate to the mask
Because the cabin altitude warning sounds through the mask
Because after a decompression you will be on the mask while you descend and talk to ATC
questions.why: The AFH high-altitude outline lists a functional test of supply and pressure, regulator, flow, mask fit, and pilot and ATC communication using mask microphones [[24:309|AFH 15-15]]. Crew masks usually contain a microphone [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]. After a decompression the mask goes on first and stays on for the descent [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]], and that is when you will be talking to ATC (application), so the microphone must work before you need it. The sources state no rule that every mask has a microphone.

questions.q: Before a Part 91 flight at FL 240, a passenger brings his own portable oxygen bottle as a backup and lays it loose on the back seat. What do you do?
options: Fasten it securely, because in an explosive decompression loose cylinders become flying debris
Leave it loose so he can reach it quickly
Nothing, since the rules for passenger oxygen bottles are only in Part 135
Put it in the aisle between the seats so either passenger can reach it
questions.why: AC 61-107B says an oxygen container should be fastened securely in the aircraft before flight [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. In an explosive decompression with a large opening, anything not secured moves toward the opening and can injure people, so baggage and oxygen cylinders must be secured [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]. Readily accessible and secured are both needed; a loose bottle is a hazard, not a convenience.

questions.q: You will practice a simulated rapid decompression and emergency descent on an IFR flight at FL 220. What does AC 61-107B say about doing it?
options: Coordinate with ATC in advance and do not leave your assigned altitude without a clearance
Start down as soon as your mask is on; ATC will see the descent on radar
Squawk 7700 so ATC clears the airspace below you
Dump the cabin briefly so the practice feels real
questions.why: The AC says never actually depressurize for training. Simulate it by donning the masks, turning on the oxygen, configuring and flying the emergency descent, coordinate with ATC in advance, and do not vacate any assigned altitude without a clearance [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. 61.31(g) also calls for a simulated rapid decompression without actually depressurizing the aircraft [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

questions.q: Why does a typical pressurization system hold the cabin at about 8,000 ft at the airplane's maximum designed cruising altitude?
options: Because 91.211 requires oxygen above an 8,000 ft cabin
It keeps cabin altitude from changing fast enough to hurt or bother people, and still lets stale air and odors be cleared
Because the AIM says 8,000 ft is the highest safe cabin altitude at night
Because no fuselage can hold more differential at any altitude
questions.why: The PHAK says holding about 8,000 ft at the maximum designed cruising altitude prevents rapid cabin altitude changes that may be uncomfortable or cause injury, and still allows a reasonably fast exchange of air to remove odors and stale air. At 8,000 ft or below, oxygen equipment is not required [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]]. The first oxygen requirement in 91.211 starts above 12,500 ft cabin altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], and the AIM's night recommendation is oxygen above 5,000 ft, not a limit at 8,000 ft [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: A Part 135 pressurized airplane will cruise at 28,000 ft. Its best emergency descent averages 2,500 fpm. What passenger oxygen supply does 135.157 require for flight above 15,000 ft?
options: A 30-minute supply for each passenger, since it can get down in about 5 minutes
A one-hour supply for each passenger, since it cannot reach 15,000 ft within 4 minutes
Oxygen for 10 percent of the passengers only
Only the 10-minute descent supply, since the airplane is pressurized
questions.why: Above 15,000 ft each passenger needs oxygen for one hour, unless at all times above that altitude the airplane can safely descend to 15,000 ft within four minutes, which cuts it to 30 minutes [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]]. (28,000 - 15,000) / 2,500 = 5.2 minutes, more than four, so the one-hour supply applies. The 10-minute supply above 25,000 ft is a separate line of the same rule [[6:60|14 CFR 135.157]], and 10 percent of passengers is the rule for 10,000 to 15,000 ft.

questions.q: Two pilots fly a pressurized single-engine jet at FL 390. Both stay at the controls, and each has a quick-donning mask that goes on with one hand within 5 seconds. What does 91.211(b) require about wearing masks?
options: Neither pilot must wear a mask while both stay at the controls
One pilot must wear a sealed mask at all times above FL 350
Both pilots must wear masks above FL 350
Masks must be worn only above FL 410 when one pilot leaves
questions.why: Above FL 350 one pilot at the controls must wear and use a sealed mask, except that at or below FL 410 neither has to if two pilots are at the controls and each has a quick-donning mask that goes on with one hand within 5 seconds [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211]]. FL 390 is inside that exception. If one pilot leaves the controls above FL 350, the other must put on and use a mask until that pilot returns [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211]], at any altitude above FL 350, not only above FL 410.

questions.q: You land after a high-altitude flight in which everyone used oxygen in the descent. Before you leave the airplane, what do the PHAK and AC 61-107B tell you to check?
options: That all oxygen components and valves are shut off
That the oxygen is left on so the lines stay purged for the next flight
That the remaining oxygen is vented so the bottle is not stored under pressure
That the masks are rinsed under running water, microphones included
questions.why: After any oxygen use, verify that all components and valves are shut off [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Before leaving the airplane, the AC's training outline says to check that all oxygen equipment and valves are off or in the position the manufacturer recommends [[11:45|AC 61-107B 2-12]]. Masks are cleaned with mild soap and water, but a built-in microphone is wiped with a swab, not running water [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
